source.title: ILASR: Privacy-Preserving Incremental Learning for Automatic Speech Recognition at Production Scale
source.authors: Gopinath Chennupati; M. Rao; Gurpreet Chadha; A. Eakin; A. Raju; Gautam Tiwari; Anit Kumar Sahu; A. Rastrow; J. Droppo; Andrew Oberlin; Buddha Nandanoor; Prahalad Venkataramanan; Zheng-Wei Wu; Pankaj Sitpure

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: Tests batch-size effects on held-out ASR performance in an incremental-learning setting, extending the batch-size question to a new modality and training setup.
record.gate_note: The paper reports batch-size results for ASR. Cited findings about image classifiers and other prior work are not this study’s results. Table 2 states that it covers three models, but the supplied table text exposes values only under rnnt_60m; no values for the other models are inferred.
record.test_reason: The study tests the batch-size question in a new setting: incremental fine-tuning of pretrained ASR models. Section 5.1.1 explicitly holds the amount of data processed constant while larger batches reduce update counts, providing an equal-data-pass comparison relevant to V5.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately captures the batch-size conclusion: increasing effective batches from 9k to approximately 300k does not meaningfully degrade held-out performance in ILASR. The authors suggest initialization from converged pretrained models explains this robustness, but do not isolate that explanation experimentally.
record.recipe_differences: Incremental fine-tuning of converged production RNN-T ASR models on machine-transcribed streaming data, measured by WERR; the batch-size comparisons use gradient accumulation and are not the cited fixed-epoch image-classification or language-model setups.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports batch-size comparisons across test sets; it states the effect on WER is insignificant.
record.peer_reviewed: KDD ’22, Proceedings of the 28th ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining
record.problems: The supplied Table 2 text exposes numerical rows only for rnnt_60m despite the caption saying all three models. No uncertainty estimates are stated. Results are WERR against pre-trained baselines rather than direct train-test gaps, and the tested setting is incremental ASR with machine transcripts.
record.rows_left_out: No rows were omitted. Table 2 values for models other than rnnt_60m are not recoverable from the supplied text.

untested.parts: Width beyond interpolation and its effect on test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local connectivity.
Comparative optimizer performance under limited or broader tuning; using Adam alone does not test this.

Image classifiers and standalone language models; training from random initialization; batches below 9k; locating a workload-dependent critical size; controlled comparisons of longer training, learning-rate scaling, warmup, normalization, or regularization changes.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, generalization gaps, and comparisons with other measures.
Removing memorized training examples versus random examples.

record.verdict_notes: Held-out WERR comparisons can test V5 without measuring a train–test gap. Equal data processing is explicit in section 5.1.1, so fixed data-pass budgets should not be listed as wholly untested. The learning-rate schedule is unchanged across batch sizes, but already includes warmup and decay; this is not a no-warmup experiment. No uncertainty estimates or formal significance tests are supplied, so 'insignificant' reflects the authors' characterization. Table 2 exposes only rnnt_60m despite its caption referring to three models; unavailable values are already declared in rows_left_out.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Widening beyond interpolation and test-error behavior.
Convolutional versus fully connected image models.
Image-classification and language models; fixed epoch budgets; training longer, learning-rate scaling with warmup, and normalization or regularization changes; train-test error gap itself.

relationships.condition: Pretrained rnnt_60m incrementally fine-tuned on machine-transcribed speech, equal data processed, effective batches 9k–307k, four test sets
relationships.reason: R1–R24 show no meaningful large-batch penalty according to the authors: Jan–Mar WERR is 2.74% at 9k versus 2.24% at 307k, Rare 3.58% versus 3.72%, Message 6.46% versus 9.37%, and General 15.14% versus 14.26%. This extends the conditions where the penalty is absent to pretrained incremental ASR.
relationships.display_finding: Reported word-error-rate reductions indicated lower error rates on Rare and Message but higher rates on Jan–Mar and General. The authors described no meaningful penalty, but the results did not establish equivalent performance once uncertainty was taken into account.

relation.reason: Table 2 directly compares held-out WERR across effective batch sizes, and Section 5.1.1 evaluates whether larger batches degrade performance.

tranche.reason: Section 5.1.1 tests batch-size effects in the new setting of incremental pretrained ASR fine-tuning, explicitly holding processed data constant while reducing update counts.

source_check.notes: Table 2 reports WERR relative to a weaker pretrained baseline than Table 1, not train–test gaps. Batch differences lack reported uncertainty establishing equivalence; the proposed explanation involving pretrained initialization is not experimentally isolated.
